title: The Vision Model That Learned to See Without Convolutions
body:
Strip every convolution out of a state-of-the-art vision model and replace it with plain attention. The result still hits 88.55% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet.

That single result is the reason this project exists: a systematic analysis of the **Vision Transformer (ViT)**, Google Research's pure attention-based architecture for large-scale image recognition. For over a decade, computer vision assumed convolution was non-negotiable — the thing that let a network "see" edges and textures before it saw objects. ViT tests that assumption directly, and the answer changes how the next generation of vision models gets built.

---

## The question CNNs weren't supposed to lose

Transformers already own natural language processing. Global self-attention lets a model relate any word to any other word, and that flexibility is what pushed NLP past recurrent networks.

Vision resisted the same move. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) dominate image tasks because they come pre-loaded with inductive biases — locality and translation equivariance — baked directly into the architecture. Early hybrid attempts that bolted attention onto CNNs produced only limited gains, and pure attention models had a consistent track record of underperforming CNNs at standard dataset scale.

So the key question this project sets out to answer is blunt: **can a Transformer-based architecture outperform CNNs in vision tasks when trained at sufficient scale?** Everything below is the attempt to answer it with data, not intuition.

---

## Turning an image into a sentence

Feed a Transformer a sentence and it processes a sequence of tokens. Feed it an image and there's no sequence — just a grid of pixels. ViT's first move is to manufacture one.

Given an input image

$$
x \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C}
$$

the image is cut into fixed-size patches of size $P \times P$, producing

$$
N = \frac{HW}{P^2}
$$

patches. Each patch is flattened and linearly projected into a latent embedding, so the whole image becomes a sequence the Transformer encoder can read:

$$
z_0 = [x_{\text{CLS}}; x_1E; x_2E; \dots; x_NE] + E_{\text{pos}}
$$

Here $x_{\text{CLS}}$ is a learnable classification token, $E$ is the patch embedding matrix, and $E_{\text{pos}}$ carries positional embeddings — the model's only hint about where each patch actually sat in the original image.

That sequence then runs through the standard Transformer encoder. Each block does three things: Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA), a Feed-Forward Network (MLP), and residual connections wrapped in Layer Normalization. For the $l$-th encoder block:

$$
z'_l = \text{MHSA}(\text{LN}(z_{l-1})) + z_{l-1}
$$

$$
z_l = \text{MLP}(\text{LN}(z'_l)) + z'_l
$$

Stack that block $L$ times, and the final hidden state at the **[CLS] token** becomes the image's global representation — the single vector an MLP head maps to class logits.

Why it matters: nothing here is vision-specific. No convolution, no pooling, no hand-designed locality. The architecture is the same Transformer encoder NLP already uses, pointed at patches instead of words.

---

## Three sizes, one recipe

An architecture is only a shape until someone scales it. ViT comes in three variants:

| Model | Layers | Hidden Dim | MLP Dim | Heads | Params |
|------|--------|------------|---------|-------|--------|
| ViT-B | 12 | 768 | 3072 | 12 | 86M |
| ViT-L | 24 | 1024 | 4096 | 16 | 307M |
| ViT-H | 32 | 1280 | 5120 | 16 | 632M |

The naming convention tells you the patch size too — ViT-L/16 means a $16 \times 16$ input patch, smaller patches meaning longer sequences and finer-grained attention.

None of these variants mean much without data to match. ViT was pretrained across:

| Dataset | Images | Classes |
|-------|--------|---------|
| ImageNet-1k | 1.3M | 1,000 |
| ImageNet-21k | 14M | 21,000 |
| JFT-300M | 303M | 18,000 |

Large-scale pretraining turns out to be **critical** to ViT's performance — not a nice-to-have. On the optimization side, SGD, Momentum, Adagrad, and Adam were all evaluated; fine-tuning consistently improved convergence stability, and Adam-based optimizers showed faster initial convergence for ViT.

The pattern underneath the numbers: a model with no built-in visual assumptions has to learn everything from exposure. Give it 303 million images and it can. Give it too few, and the missing inductive bias starts to show.

---

## The numbers that settle the question

This is where the key question gets an answer. Across five benchmarks, ViT variants sit alongside two strong CNN baselines — BiT-L and Noisy Student:

| Dataset | ViT-H/14 (JFT) | ViT-L/16 (JFT) | ViT-L/16 (IN21k) | BiT-L | Noisy Student |
|-------|---------------|---------------|------------------|-------|---------------|
| ImageNet | 88.55 ± 0.04 | 87.76 ± 0.03 | 85.30 ± 0.02 | 87.54 ± 0.02 | 88.4 |
| ImageNet ReaL | 90.72 ± 0.05 | 90.54 ± 0.03 | 88.62 ± 0.05 | 90.54 | 90.55 |
| CIFAR-10 | 99.50 ± 0.06 | 99.42 ± 0.03 | 99.15 ± 0.03 | 99.37 ± 0.06 | – |
| CIFAR-100 | 94.55 ± 0.04 | 93.90 ± 0.05 | 93.25 ± 0.05 | 93.51 ± 0.08 | – |
| VTAB (19 tasks) | 77.63 ± 0.23 | 76.28 ± 0.46 | 72.72 ± 0.21 | 76.29 ± 1.70 | – |

ViT-H/14 matches or edges out both CNN baselines on every row. That alone answers the key question. But the more striking number is sitting in a different table — compute cost:

| Model | TPUv3 Core-Days |
|-----|------------------|
| ViT-H/14 (JFT) | 2.5k |
| ViT-L/16 (JFT) | 0.68k |
| ViT-L/16 (IN21k) | 0.23k |
| BiT-L | 9.9k |
| Noisy Student | 12.3k |

ViT reaches competitive or superior accuracy at a fraction of the pretraining cost — ViT-H/14 uses roughly a quarter of BiT-L's core-days, and ViT-L/16 (IN21k) uses less than a fortieth of Noisy Student's.

On VTAB's 19 tasks — spanning natural, specialized, and structured categories — ViT transfers well across all three, which is the clearest sign that global self-attention is learning general-purpose visual representations rather than overfitting to ImageNet's specific quirks.

Pull the observations together and a consistent story appears: ViT matches or exceeds CNN-based state-of-the-art once pretraining is large-scale. The absence of strong inductive bias raises data dependency, but it buys flexibility in return. Self-supervised and large-scale pretraining aren't optional extras — they're the mechanism. And attention-based models scale more predictably than convolutional ones, which is the kind of property that matters more with every doubling of dataset size.

---

## What this changes

The one idea worth keeping: convolution was never a law of vision, it was a shortcut — a useful bias that substitutes for data when data is scarce. Once data and compute are abundant enough, a generic attention mechanism can learn the same regularities on its own, and it learns them in a way that transfers.

If you're evaluating architectures for a vision task, don't ask "does this need convolution" — ask how much labeled data and compute you actually have. That answer, more than the architecture diagram, is what will decide whether pure attention outperforms a CNN for you.
